extracted.intended_audience: political scientists, policy researchers, and students studying agency rulemaking, interest group mobilization, and notice-and-comment processes
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and standards for identifying, coding, and measuring mass (public pressure) comment campaigns and their effects on agency rulemaking; includes rules for classifying comment positions, coalitions, campaign scale, coalition types, and measuring lobbying success and mechanisms of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding nuanced comment positions (support/oppose/less/more)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify each comment's spatial position relative to the proposed rule: e.g., comments that explicitly oppose the proposed rule are coded as opposing (p_i = x1); unqualified support or requests for more policy change are coded as supporting (p_i = x2 or p_i > x2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments that 'applaud EPA’s efforts to regulate, but would prefer less severe limits' are coded as supporting the rule but asking for less change. If a commenter opposes a proposed rule because it is insufficient (e.g., urging withdrawal unless revised), take the comment at face value and code it as opposition even if its spatial position is closer to the proposed rule than the current policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assigning coalition position
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign each coalition's position as the position of the lead organization; for robustness, also compute the coalition's average position as the mean position of its members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coalition members usually have nearly identical positions; when some members ask for additional changes, consider divergent interests part of one coalition only if those asks are entirely compatible with the position of organizations that did not ask for them. Conflicting policy demands indicate different coalitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis: use coalitions not organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the lobbying coalition — not individual organizations — as the appropriate unit of analysis for mass comment campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measuring campaigns at the organization level can vastly overcount the same campaign when many organizations are part of a single coalition (e.g., counting one coalition as 40 separate 'campaigns'). Using coalitions avoids non-independence and more accurately measures levels of public pressure per coalition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of mass comments to sponsoring organizations/coalitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute mass (mobilized) comments to the organizations and coalitions that organize them, including those that also submit sophisticated technical comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat mass comments as independent from the sophisticated lobbying they often accompany; instead, attribute both types of comments to the broader lobbying effort so that mass comments are measured as part of coalition-level mobilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of mass comments (duplication threshold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify comments into categories by duplication: mass comments are those with large numbers of identical or reused texts; the study treats 'mass comments' as 100 or more form letters or copied text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partially unique and small batches (less than 100) are a tiny fraction of total comments and should be distinguished from mass campaigns; use text-reuse detection and thresholds to separate mass, partially unique, and unique/sophisticated comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring campaign scale (metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify campaigns using counts and summary statistics: total comments mobilized, average comments per campaign, average comments per coalition, percent of rules with a campaign, and organization-level averages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples reported include total comments, average comments (e.g., public interest campaign average = 205,183; private interest = 50,241), and share of comments mobilized by top organizations. Use tables and figures to report totals, averages, and distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying top mobilizers
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and rank organizations by the number of comments they mobilize and by the share/average mobilized per campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both absolute counts (total comments mobilized) and campaign-level metrics (average per campaign, percent of rules where pressure campaigns were used). Note that many top mobilizers are also sophisticated lobbying organizations and often act as coalition leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifying coalition type: public interest vs private interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify coalitions as public-interest-led or private-interest-led based on coalition membership and leadership (e.g., environmental NGOs vs industry associations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public interest coalitions tend to mobilize more comments on average and more total comments; private interest coalitions are less likely to run public pressure campaigns and more likely to mobilize mainly in response to opposing public interest campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining whether a campaign is opposed or unopposed
rubrics_metrics.description: Record whether a coalition's pressure campaign faced counter-mobilization from opposing coalitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private interest coalitions are less likely to run unopposed campaigns; public interest coalitions often run unopposed. Report counts of coalition-level campaigns that were opposed vs unopposed as an indicator of the competitive environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying astroturf vs grassroots characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether mobilized comments reflect grassroots participation or astroturfing based on attributes such as organizer transparency, anonymity, and the presence of sponsoring organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Astroturf campaigns are often anonymous and less likely to name sponsor organizations; because coalition-led campaigns commonly include sophisticated lobbying teams, astroturf is less common than expected. Note limitations: anonymity makes astroturf harder to detect, and astroturf may be concentrated where public pressure is most decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal/partisan analysis of support vs opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze changes over time and across administrations in the balance of comments supporting vs opposing proposed rules, and validate hand-coded patterns with alternative machine coding (e.g., presence of words 'support'/'oppose').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: hand-coded sample shows more 'support' mentions in Obama years and more 'oppose' in Trump years; validate with automated word-based measures as robustness checks and be aware of timing differences in alternative measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for measuring lobbying success
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure lobbying success at the coalition level by: (1) developing computational methods to identify lobbying coalitions; (2) hand-coding a random sample of rules to determine whether each coalition achieved its desired policy outcome; and (3) modeling the relationship between campaign scale and outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include robustness checks for selection effects (e.g., coalitions may mobilize because they expect success). Use both hand-coding and computational identification to link mobilization to policy outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing mechanisms of influence (direct vs indirect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish whether public pressure affects agency decisionmakers directly or indirectly via elected officials (e.g., members of Congress) by measuring mediator variables such as congressional engagement/oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether legislators are more likely to engage in rulemaking when advocacy groups mobilize public pressure and test whether legislative engagement mediates the relationship between mobilization and lobbying success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed-methods approach: combine hand-coding and computational text analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a mixture of hand-coding (to capture nuanced positions and outcomes) and computational text-reuse/detection methods (to identify scale and identical submissions) to capture different levels of public pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hand-code spatial positions and outcomes on a random sample for validity; use text-reuse algorithms to detect mass comment duplication at scale and attribute reused text to sponsoring organizations/coalitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing normative representativeness of mobilized participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the normative value of public participation by comparing the constituencies organizations claim to represent with the actual participants mobilized in campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend probing representation via linking campaigns to survey data or other population-representative measures to test whether mobilized commenters reflect broader public opinion or are misaligned/misinformed or geographically unrepresentative (e.g., national sign-ons claiming to represent a local affected area).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize research design limitations and selection concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the possibility that decisions to mobilize are endogenous to expected lobbying success (i.e., coalitions may mobilize when they anticipate success), which can confound causal claims about the effect of mobilization on outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use robustness checks and mediational analyses (e.g., via congressional engagement) to separate selection from causal effects; explicitly discuss limitations in inference when coalitions self-select into mobilizing.
